pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: The combination of severe abdominal pain with a benign abdomen, light-dependent port-wine urine coloration, SIADH-induced hyponatremia, and sudden catastrophic neuromuscular paralysis triggered by a potent CYP450 inducer (phenytoin). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant disorder of heme biosynthesis caused by a deficiency in porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD / HMBS). Caloric restriction and cytochrome P450-inducing drugs (such as phenytoin) deplete regulatory hepatic heme pools, profoundly upregulating the rate-limiting enzyme delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1). This drives a massive accumulation of the neurotoxic heme intermediates delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). ALA causes severe central, autonomic, and peripheral neurotoxicity: dysautonomia drives hypertension and tachycardia, hypothalamic injury results in SIADH, visceral autonomic neuropathy presents as pseudo-obstruction and abdominal pain, and peripheral motor neuropathy causes an ascending flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain-Barré syndrome. PBG oxidizes and polymerizes into porphobilin and porphyrins under room light, turning the urine port-wine red. Administration of phenytoin was fatal fuel to the fire, drastically amplifying ALAS1 induction. Urgent management requires stopping all porphyrinogenic agents, administering intravenous carbohydrates, and infusing intravenous hemin to shut down ALAS1 transcription via negative feedback.
